vocabularies.ISO/IEC 27001:2022: clause 3 defines no terms; it delegates to ISO/IEC 27000

rows.name: Machine Learning
rows.description: Building systems that learn patterns from data rather than being explicitly programmed.

rows.name: AI Agent
rows.description: A single AI system that acts toward a goal - it can plan, use tools, and take steps rather than only answering.

rows.name: Risk Evaluation
rows.description: Judging acceptability against tolerance.

rows.name: Residual Risk
rows.description: The risk remaining after treatment.

rows.name: Measure
rows.description: Assess, analyze, and track identified risks.

rows.name: Risk Analysis
rows.description: Understanding a risk's nature, likelihood, and severity.

rows.name: Risk Identification
rows.description: Determining what could go wrong and to whom.

rows.name: Risk Treatment
rows.description: Acting to modify a risk to an acceptable level.

rows.name: AI System Impact Assessment
rows.description: Evaluating an AI system's effects on individuals, groups, and society.

rows.name: AI System
rows.description: A machine-based system that infers from input how to generate outputs influencing environments.

rows.name: Audit scope
rows.description: That an audit covers a named tool, configuration, population and date, and nothing outside them.

rows.name: Documented information
rows.description: What the standard requires plus what the organization judges necessary, with its extent varying by size, process complexity and the competence of people. More documentation is not better documentation.

rows.name: AI system life cycle
rows.description: The span obligations attach to, reaching from development through transfer and decommissioning. It is why throughout its life cycle recurs across the control objectives, and why deployment is not the finish line.

rows.name: Audit programme
rows.description: Covers methods, frequency, responsibilities, reporting and planning, and considers the importance of the processes audited and what earlier audits found. Evidence is required of the programme's implementation as well as of its results.

rows.name: AI system impact assessment
rows.description: Reaches past intended use into foreseeable misuse, and past the organization into societies. Its results are a required input to the risk assessment, and clause 8.4 requires it performed at planned intervals and on significant change.

rows.name: Data quality
rows.description: Defined requirements the data used to develop and operate the system must meet, with the effect of bias on performance and fairness weighed and the model or data adjusted. Distinct from integrity, which only says nobody unauthorised altered it.

rows.name: Nonconformity
rows.description: Includes failing the organization's own policy, objectives and documented processes, and requirements that are generally implied rather than written. In a young field much of what is reasonably expected has not been written down and is a requirement anyway.

rows.name: Continual improvement
rows.description: Clause 10.1's obligation, covering the system's suitability, adequacy and effectiveness. Three separate paths lead from this is not working back to a decision, and using none of them means waiting for internal audit, the slowest instrument there is.

rows.name: Statement of applicability
rows.description: Not a control register: all identified risks and the measures addressing them must be reflected in it, which makes each entry traceable to the risk that required it. Every Annex A control must be addressed, and absence is neither inclusion nor exclusion.

rows.name: Risk criteria
rows.description: Clause 6.1.2 requires the risk assessment process to identify, analyse and evaluate AI risks, which presupposes criteria against which risks are evaluated. The auditor tests the process against the criteria the organization itself established, since clause 9.2.1 makes the organization's own requirements for its AIMS part of the audit criteria alongside the standard.

rows.name: Audit scope
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.6 defines audit scope as the extent and boundaries of an audit, with a note that it generally includes a description of the physical and virtual locations, functions, organizational units, activities and processes, and the time period covered. For an AI management system audit the virtual locations and the specific AI systems in scope matter as much as the organizational units, and a scope that names neither cannot later be tested against a finding.

rows.name: Internal audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.1 defines an audit as a systematic, independent and documented process for obtaining objective evidence and evaluating it objectively to determine the extent to which the audit criteria are fulfilled. Note 2 to entry adds that an internal audit is conducted by, or on behalf of, the organization itself. An organization may therefore engage a contracted auditor and the audit remains a first-party audit; what makes it internal is whose management system is being examined, not who holds the pen.

rows.name: Audit criteria
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.8 defines audit criteria as the set of requirements used as a reference against which objective evidence is compared. A note records that requirements may include policies, procedures, work instructions, legal requirements and contractual obligations, and a further note that where the criteria are legal requirements the words compliance and non-compliance are often used in a finding. For this credential the criteria are ISO/IEC 42001:2023 together with the organization's own AI management system requirements, as clause 9.2.1 of that standard sets out.

rows.name: Governing Body
rows.description: the group accountable for the organization's direction and control.

rows.name: Residual risk
rows.description: the risk remaining after treatment

rows.name: Risk identification
rows.description: finding, recognizing and describing risks

rows.name: Nonconformity
rows.description: a failure to meet a requirement

rows.name: Access control
rows.description: restricting access to information and processing facilities

rows.name: Audit criteria
rows.description: the requirements against which conformity is judged

rows.name: Threat
rows.description: a potential cause of an unwanted incident

rows.name: Risk evaluation
rows.description: comparing analysis results against criteria to decide significance

rows.name: Top management
rows.description: the level at which ISMS accountability ultimately sits

rows.name: Continual improvement
rows.description: the ongoing obligation to improve suitability, adequacy and effectiveness

rows.name: Vulnerability
rows.description: a weakness that can be exploited by a threat

rows.name: Risk analysis
rows.description: understanding the nature of a risk and determining its level

rows.name: Risk criteria
rows.description: the terms of reference against which risk significance is judged

rows.name: Risk owner
rows.description: the person accountable for a specific risk and its treatment

rows.name: Statement of applicability
rows.description: the documented record of which controls are necessary and why

rows.name: Availability
rows.description: information is accessible and usable on demand by an authorized entity

rows.name: Confidentiality
rows.description: information is not made available to unauthorized individuals, entities or processes

rows.name: Integrity
rows.description: information is accurate and complete and has not been altered without authorization

rows.name: Audit finding
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.11 defines an audit finding as the result of evaluating collected audit evidence against the audit criteria.

rows.name: Combined audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.2 defines a combined audit as one carried out together at a single auditee on two or more management systems.

rows.name: Audit evidence
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.10 defines audit evidence as records, statements of fact or other information which are relevant to the audit criteria and verifiable.

rows.name: Audit programme
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.5 defines it as arrangements for a set of one or more audits planned for a specific time frame and directed towards a specific purpose.

rows.name: Audit scope
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.6 defines audit scope as the extent and boundaries of an audit, generally including physical and virtual locations, functions, organizational units, activities and processes, and the time period covered.

rows.name: Documented information
rows.description: Clause 7.5 covers what the ISMS must include (7.5.1), creating and updating (7.5.2), and control (7.5.3), including documented information of external origin the organization determines is necessary.

rows.name: Audit criteria
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.8 defines audit criteria as the set of requirements used as a reference against which objective evidence is compared - which may include policies, procedures, legal requirements, contractual obligations and standards.

rows.name: Remote auditing method
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.4 defines it as a method for conducting audit activities from any place other than the location of the auditee. The definition is sourced from ISO/IEC TS 17012:2024, whose guidance the 2026 edition imports.

rows.name: Transparency
rows.description: Making the true state of the work visible.

rows.name: Transparency
rows.description: First pillar of empirical process control; the prerequisite for inspection.

rows.name: Transparency
rows.description: The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving it; artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

rows.name: Acceptable-Use Policy
rows.description: Organizational rules on approved tools, permitted data, disclosure, and prohibited uses.

rows.name: AI Bias
rows.description: Systematic skew in AI output that disadvantages some people or groups.

rows.name: Technical-Documentation Requirement
rows.description: Documentation demonstrating the system meets requirements.

rows.name: Meaningful Human Control
rows.description: Retaining genuine control over consequential autonomous action.

rows.name: Acceptable vs Unacceptable Risk
rows.description: The threshold separating risks borne from those refused.

rows.name: Harmful Bias
rows.description: Outputs systematically and unfairly disadvantaging individuals or groups.

rows.name: Harmful-Content Risk
rows.description: Generation of dangerous, violent, abusive, or harmful material.

rows.name: Limited Risk (Transparency)
rows.description: Systems subject mainly to transparency and disclosure duties.

rows.name: Minimal Risk
rows.description: The majority of AI systems; no specific obligations.

rows.name: Systemic-Risk Model
rows.description: The most capable GPAI models carrying additional obligations.

rows.name: AI Policy
rows.description: The organization's documented commitment and rules for AI.

rows.name: Data-Governance Requirement
rows.description: Training, validation, and test data quality and governance requirements.

rows.name: Information Integrity
rows.description: Generative AI's effect on the information ecosystem (misinformation, deepfakes).

rows.name: Post-Market Monitoring
rows.description: Ongoing surveillance of a deployed system's real-world performance.

rows.name: AI Risk Management
rows.description: The ongoing process of identifying, analyzing, evaluating, and treating AI risk.

rows.name: Data-Privacy Risk
rows.description: Exposure or misuse of personal data via training data or outputs.

rows.name: Meaningful human review
rows.description: Review by a person with authority to change the outcome, access to the underlying data, and time to use both - as distinct from a rubber stamp.

rows.name: AI management system
rows.description: What ISO/IEC 42001 actually places requirements on. It governs how an organization decides, documents and checks its use of AI, and says nothing about what a model must do.

rows.name: AI risk assessment
rows.description: Anchored to the AI policy and objectives, and its analysis assesses consequences to the organization, individuals and societies - all three. It is not the organization-only half of a pair with the impact assessment.

rows.name: AI risk criteria
rows.description: Established before any assessment runs, and required to support four things: separating acceptable from unacceptable, running assessments, treating the result, and assessing risk impacts. The fourth wires clause 6.1.4 in before it appears.

rows.name: Internal audit requirement
rows.description: Tests conformity against the organization's own requirements as well as the standard's, and whether the system is effectively implemented and maintained. A finding can be entirely legitimate without pointing at any clause of the standard.

rows.name: AI policy
rows.description: Frames the objectives, commits to meeting requirements and to continual improvement, and must reference the other policies AI intersects. One referencing none describes an organization that has none; one with no exception route is ignored at a deadline.

rows.name: External reporting control
rows.description: A route for interested parties to flag harm the system has done - interested parties, not only users. A person the system acted on may have no account, no contract, and no obvious way to reach the organization at all.

rows.name: AI risk treatment
rows.description: Controls are determined first from the chosen treatment options, and Annex A enters afterwards as a comparison to catch what was missed. Opening the annex first inverts the logic and leaves no link from risk to control for an auditor to test.

rows.name: Internal audit and certification audit
rows.description: An internal audit under ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.2 provides the organization with information on whether its AI management system conforms to its own requirements and to the standard, and is effectively implemented and maintained. A certification audit is conducted by an external body to decide whether to grant a certificate. They differ in who requests them, who reports to whom, and what follows: an internal audit produces findings for the organization to act on, and no certificate.

rows.name: Meaningful Human Control
rows.description: retaining genuine control over consequential autonomous action.

rows.name: Data Availability for Prediction
rows.description: whether enough quality historical/operational data exists to predict reliably.

rows.name: AI Service Monitoring
rows.description: ongoing observation of an AI-driven service's real-world behavior.

rows.name: AI Model Supplier Risk
rows.description: an AI service often runs on a foundation model owned by an external provider, concentrating critical dependency in a supplier.

rows.name: Information classification
rows.description: assigning and handling information by sensitivity

rows.name: Internal audit programme
rows.description: the planned programme of internal audits

rows.name: Ai risk identification
rows.description: surfacing information risks specific to an AI deployment

rows.name: Security event
rows.description: an identified occurrence indicating a possible security-relevant state

rows.name: Security property attribute
rows.description: which of confidentiality, integrity or availability a control serves

rows.name: Security control
rows.description: An answer to a risk the organization chose not to accept; judged by whether the risk moved, not by whether the control is present.

rows.name: AI evaluation tools in auditor competence
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 7.2.3 item 10 gives artificial-intelligence-based evaluation tools as its example of the technology an auditor must understand the appropriateness and consequences of using. The competence is about the AI tool in the auditor's own hands, not about auditing AI.

rows.name: AI Code Review
rows.description: The extra scrutiny AI-authored code demands.

rows.name: Fairness Awareness
rows.description: Noticing where AI output could produce unfair treatment.

rows.name: Disclosure and Transparency
rows.description: Telling people when AI was materially used to produce work.

rows.name: Large Language Model
rows.description: A foundation model trained on text that predicts and generates language.

rows.name: Bias from Data
rows.description: Bias largely originates in training data and is reproduced by the model.

rows.name: Foundation Model
rows.description: A large general-purpose model trained broadly and adapted to many downstream uses.

rows.name: Training vs Inference
rows.description: Training is learning from data; inference is using the trained model to answer.

rows.name: Human Review
rows.description: A person reads, judges, and takes responsibility for the output before it is used.

rows.name: Bias Mitigation
rows.description: Measuring and reducing harmful bias.

rows.name: Explainability for Stakeholders
rows.description: Providing explanations appropriate to the audience.

rows.name: Fairness in AI
rows.description: Equitable treatment across individuals and groups.

rows.name: ISO/IEC 23894 (Risk)
rows.description: Companion guidance on AI risk management.

rows.name: Control Selection
rows.description: Choosing controls proportionate to likelihood and severity.

rows.name: Human-Oversight Requirement
rows.description: High-risk systems must enable effective human oversight.

rows.name: IP and Provenance Risk
rows.description: Infringement, attribution, and origin issues in generated content.

rows.name: Management-System Standard
rows.description: A certifiable standard defining an auditable organizational system.

rows.name: Risk-Management-System Requirement
rows.description: A documented, ongoing risk-management process is required.

rows.name: Risk-Treatment Options
rows.description: The set of possible responses to a risk.

rows.name: Iterative Risk Process
rows.description: The process repeats across the lifecycle as context changes.

rows.name: Policy to Practice
rows.description: How policy translates into day-to-day AI decisions.

rows.name: Risk Prioritization
rows.description: Ranking risks so effort targets the most significant first.

rows.name: Sources of Bias
rows.description: How bias enters AI via data, design, and deployment.

rows.name: Data Quality and Representativeness
rows.description: Data fit for purpose and representative of the affected population.

rows.name: Management-System Certification
rows.description: What independent third-party certification to a management standard signals.

rows.name: Risk Tolerance
rows.description: The level of risk an organization accepts to pursue objectives.

rows.name: Transparency Duty
rows.description: The obligation to be open about AI use and behavior.

rows.name: AI System Lifecycle
rows.description: The stages an AI system passes through from conception to retirement.

rows.name: Conformity Assessment
rows.description: The process to demonstrate a high-risk system meets the requirements.

rows.name: Impact vs Risk Assessment
rows.description: Impact assessment (effects on people) vs risk assessment (threats to objectives).

rows.name: Likelihood and Severity
rows.description: The two axes by which AI risk is characterized and prioritized.

rows.name: Oversight as a Control
rows.description: Human oversight as a designed, primary risk control for consequential AI.

rows.name: Agentic Risk
rows.description: Risk from systems that plan and act autonomously across steps and tools.

rows.name: Autonomy Risk
rows.description: Risk from an AI system taking consequential action with reduced human intervention.

rows.name: Model Card
rows.description: A standardized summary of a model's characteristics, intended use, and limitations.

rows.name: Model Drift
rows.description: Degradation of a deployed model's performance as conditions shift over time.

rows.name: Ongoing Monitoring
rows.description: Continuous observation of a deployed system to detect drift and emerging risks.

rows.name: Risk-Based Approach
rows.description: Obligations scale with the risk a use poses, not the technology itself.

rows.name: Risk vs Harm
rows.description: A harm is a realized negative impact; a risk is the possibility of a harm.

rows.name: Foundation / General-Purpose Model
rows.description: A broadly-capable model adaptable to many tasks (the GPAI the EU AI Act singles out).

rows.name: Audit recency
rows.description: That model or configuration updates can invalidate a prior audit.

rows.name: Audit trail
rows.description: The traceable sequence showing how a decision was reached and by whom.

rows.name: Task-based requirement
rows.description: Specifying capability as something observable the person must be able to do.

rows.name: Auditor independence
rows.description: Whether the auditing party is genuinely independent of the vendor whose tool is audited.

rows.name: Candidate data confidentiality
rows.description: That resumes, interview notes, salary data and background information are personal data owed protection.

rows.name: Fabricated requirement
rows.description: Requirements, benefits, salary bands or legal language invented by a model and never approved.

rows.name: Verification of record
rows.description: The issuer-held record that is the authoritative source for whether a credential exists.

rows.name: Audit is not indemnity
rows.description: That an audit is evidence of diligence, not a transfer of liability to the vendor.

rows.name: Candidate-facing transparency
rows.description: Explaining AI involvement to a candidate plainly, without overstating either its role or its rigour.

rows.name: Credential verification
rows.description: Confirming a credential with the issuer of record rather than accepting a document or image.

rows.name: Audit population mismatch
rows.description: That the audited applicant pool may not resemble the deployer's own, limiting what the audit establishes locally.

rows.name: Requirement elicitation
rows.description: Running a requisition intake that surfaces the underlying business problem rather than the manager's guess at a title.

rows.name: Independent bias audit
rows.description: A requirement to have a covered tool audited by an independent party and, in some regimes, to publish a summary.

rows.name: Tool classification
rows.description: The act of determining whether a given system in a given workflow is in or out of scope; the gate on every downstream obligation.

rows.name: AI customer role
rows.description: The organization obtaining and using AI, end users included. Holding it exempts you from nothing: a customer for one system is routinely a producer for another.

rows.name: AI subject role
rows.description: Those the system acts on, data subjects among them. The one role an organization does not choose, and the reason impact assessment reaches people who never interact with the system.

rows.name: Integrated management system
rows.description: Reusing the machinery, one audit programme and one management review and one documented-information control, after checking what it now governs. Reusing it without checking is assumption rather than integration.

rows.name: Review records
rows.description: Evidence of the results, which means the decisions rather than the discussion. An auditor asking what the review decided and receiving a narrative of what was presented has found something.

rows.name: AI partner role
rows.description: System integrators and data providers, alongside the system rather than in it. The category exists because responsibilities have to be allocated to parties who are neither the supplier nor the user.

rows.name: Awareness requirement
rows.description: Three items: the policy, what you contribute to making the system effective including what better performance buys, and the implications of not conforming. The second is the one awareness material routinely drops.

rows.name: Integrated audit programme
rows.description: The standard's definition of audit contemplates a combined audit across two or more disciplines, so one programme, one review cycle, one nonconformity process and one reporting route can serve both systems.

rows.name: Management system standard
rows.description: A standard specifying what an organization must decide and be able to show, not what its technology must do. It is why no fairness metric is mandated anywhere in ISO/IEC 42001.

rows.name: Monitoring and measurement
rows.description: Four determinations: what, which methods, when it happens, and when results are analysed. Data collected continuously and looked at annually is being collected rather than monitored, and the two are separate decisions.

rows.name: Policy controls
rows.description: Document the policy, align it with the other policies AI intersects, and review it at planned intervals. The review consumes management review results, which closes a loop back to clause 9.3.

rows.name: AI provider role
rows.description: The organization supplying AI to others, as a platform or as a product or service. Controls about supplying documentation to third parties land here, and an organization that supplies nothing may exclude them.

rows.name: Competence evidence
rows.description: Documented information must be available to show it. Sending people on a course is the action; establishing that they can now do the thing is the requirement, and only the second is evidence.

rows.name: Residual risk approval
rows.description: Designated management approves the treatment plan and accepts what remains. Where assurance is simply unobtainable, as with a foundation model, the honest treatment records the limit and has someone with authority accept it.

rows.name: Risk analysis and evaluation
rows.description: Analysis determines consequences, likelihood where applicable, and levels; evaluation compares against the criteria and prioritizes for treatment. Likelihood is the wrong instrument for some AI risks, so the criteria must handle consequence alone.

rows.name: Impact feeds risk
rows.description: Clause 6.1.4 requires the impact assessment's results to be taken into account when risk is assessed. It is an input rather than a parallel process, and considering it is a shall.

rows.name: Continuous learning behaviour
rows.description: Behaviour that moves by design, because output and production data are fed back into training. Where it is in use, monitoring has to confirm the system still meets its design goals on real production data.

rows.name: Policy vs objective
rows.description: A policy states intent and direction; an objective is a result to be achieved. We will use AI responsibly is a policy statement and cannot be an objective, because nothing about it can be monitored.

rows.name: Review results
rows.description: Decisions about improvement opportunities and about any changes the system needs. Both are decisions rather than summaries of discussion, and where a change is decided, clause 6.3 governs carrying it out in a planned manner.

rows.name: Top management commitment
rows.description: Clause 5.1 lists eight demonstrations and each is testable, including integrating AIMS requirements into business processes and supporting other roles to lead within their own areas. A statement of support is not among the eight.

rows.name: Control categories
rows.description: Policies, internal organization, resources, impact assessment, life cycle, data, information for interested parties, use, and third-party and customer relationships. They do not map onto ISO/IEC 27001's four themes, and mapping them is the error.

rows.name: Control count
rows.description: Thirty-eight controls, distributed unevenly, with the life cycle category holding nine across its two subdivisions. Nine categories carry ten objectives because A.6 subdivides and each half states its own, which is why published summaries disagree.

rows.name: Control overlap
rows.description: Largest where an AI control is really an information security control applied to an AI asset: protecting models and datasets, records governance, incident machinery, named AI security threats. Smallest where security has no concept of the thing.

rows.name: Management review
rows.description: Top management, not a working group reporting to them, confirming the system is still suitable, adequate and effective. Those three are not synonyms, and a review that does not separate them has usually answered only the last.

rows.name: Work under organizational control
rows.description: The scope of both competence and awareness, and it is wider than the payroll. Contractors, agency staff and consultants operating a system on the organization's behalf are all inside it if they can affect AI performance.

rows.name: AIMS effectiveness vs system performance
rows.description: Performance carries both senses here: what using the AI systems achieves, and how the management system itself is doing. A diagnostic - if every model performed perfectly for a year, would your monitoring show whether the management system worked?

rows.name: Audit criteria and scope
rows.description: Defined per audit, not once for the programme. An audit without a stated scope produces findings nobody can situate, and a combined audit plan listing only information security criteria has not covered the AIMS whatever else it examined.

rows.name: Competence does not carry
rows.description: Clause 7.2 is identical in both standards and the competence it requires is not. A security team's records evidence security competence and say nothing about whether anyone can tell that a model's output is wrong.

rows.name: Correction vs corrective action
rows.description: Correction contains the instance and deals with the consequences; corrective action removes what caused it. The clause requires both, and asks not only whether the failure will recur here but whether similar ones exist or could occur elsewhere.

rows.name: Effectiveness review
rows.description: The effectiveness of any corrective action taken must be reviewed, and actions must be appropriate to the effects encountered. Over-responding degrades the system by making it expensive to follow, which is the less obvious half of proportionality.

rows.name: Model supply chain
rows.description: For a foundation model reached as a service, several assurance questions have no available mechanism: training data and rights, what was filtered, pre-release evaluation, what the provider retains. No clause creates a capability that does not exist.

rows.name: Operational planning and control
rows.description: Controls selected during treatment must be implemented, their effectiveness monitored, and corrective action considered where results do not follow. A control chosen, deployed and never looked at again satisfies clause 6.1.3 and fails clause 8.1.

rows.name: Process criteria
rows.description: The answer to how would we know this process ran properly: which approvals, what validation evidence, what acceptable ranges, who signs off. Without them, control degenerates into an experienced person forming a view, which no auditor can test.

rows.name: Review inputs
rows.description: Prior actions, changes in issues, changes in interested-party needs, performance including trends, and improvement opportunities. Trends is the word doing the work: a single period's figures cannot show movement, which is what determines whether to act.

rows.name: Role determination requirement
rows.description: Clause 4.1 says shall, not should, and the answer is per AI system rather than per organization. It has no counterpart in ISO/IEC 27001, where how you relate to an asset does not change your obligations.

rows.name: Statement of Applicability and Annex A
rows.description: Runs in one direction: controls are determined from the treatment options, then compared against the annex to verify nothing necessary was omitted. The inverted approach produces a document of similar length with no link from risk to control.

rows.name: AI producer role
rows.description: The widest of the six categories: developers, designers, testers, deployers, procurers, impact assessors and oversight professionals all sit inside it. Treating developer as a peer category is how an organization concludes a role does not apply when it does.

rows.name: Auditor competence limit
rows.description: An ISMS auditor is not automatically competent to audit an AIMS, and that same limit is why ISO/IEC 42006 sets competence requirements for certification bodies. The gap applies to the certifier exactly as it applies to the organization.

rows.name: Intended use control
rows.description: The system is used according to its instructions and documentation, and the data it runs on aligns with them. Where correct deployment still causes concern about impact or legal requirements, the guidance directs raising it with the supplier too.

rows.name: Management system certification basis
rows.description: Not in ISO/IEC 42001 at all. ISO/IEC 42006 governs the bodies that certify an AIMS and ISO/IEC 17021-1 carries the two-stage audit and surveillance cycle; clause 9.2 is internal audit, a different activity.

rows.name: Risk vs impact assessment
rows.description: The intuitive split - risk to us, impact to them - is contradicted by the text twice. An organization that believes the two are parallel builds two disconnected processes, and the impact work never reaches the decisions the risk work drives.

rows.name: Verification validation controls
rows.description: Measures and the criteria for using them, covering test data and how well it represents the intended domain, release criteria and acceptable error rates. The guidance anticipates a system that cannot meet its criteria and directs a deliberate decision.

rows.name: Performance reporting authority
rows.description: The second named assignment, and it exists so leadership cannot be uninformed by accident. Top management must ensure the AIMS achieves its results and must review it, and neither is possible if news arrives only after something has gone wrong.

rows.name: Risk identification AI
rows.description: Annex C's risk sources reach what a conventional IT assessment does not, because that assessment asks what could go wrong with a system behaving as specified. Several of these concern one behaving exactly as built and still doing harm.

rows.name: Scope as documented information
rows.description: Define the boundary by criteria a reader could apply to a system they encountered, not by a list of systems, because the estate moves faster than the document. Exclusions are where an auditor looks first, since the reasoning is testable.

rows.name: Auditor objectivity
rows.description: The requirement attaches to the process rather than to the character of the individuals, so asserting it does not achieve it. An internal audit may be conducted by an external party on the organization's behalf, which the standard contemplates directly.

rows.name: Competence requirements AI
rows.description: Scoped to persons doing work under the organization's control rather than to employees, so a contractor labelling data or an agency operating a deployed system is inside it. Where action is taken to acquire competence, its effectiveness must be evaluated.

rows.name: Incident communication control
rows.description: A determined and documented plan for telling users. AI incidents can be specific to the system or be information security or privacy events, and integrating them into existing incident management works only if what is unique to AI stays in view.

rows.name: Control of documented information
rows.description: Available and fit to use where needed, and protected against lost confidentiality, misuse and lost integrity. Permission to view and authority to change are different grants, and conflating them is how a record gets edited by someone meant only to read it.

rows.name: Event log controls
rows.description: A determination duty with a floor: decide at which life cycle phases logs are kept, with in-use as the stated minimum. Logging everything satisfies it no better than logging nothing, because what is required is a decision per phase that can be explained.

rows.name: Clause 4.3 scope of the AI management system
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 4.3 requires the organization to determine the boundaries and applicability of the AI management system to establish its scope, considering the external and internal issues from 4.1 and the requirements of interested parties from 4.2. The scope is documented information.

rows.name: Monitoring the audit programme
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.6 covers monitoring the audit programme, and clause 5.5.6 the managing of audit programme results. Monitoring asks whether the programme is being implemented as planned and whether it is achieving its objectives, which is a different question from whether any individual audit was conducted well.

rows.name: Linking evidence to requirement
rows.description: The link is what a finding is. Evidence without a requirement is an observation; a requirement without evidence is an assertion. Annex A.18.3 c) asks for a declaration of nonconformity including a description explaining why the audit criteria are not fulfilled, which is the link stated explicitly rather than left for the reader to infer.

rows.name: Clause 9.3 management review
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.3.1 requires top management to review the organization's AI management system at planned intervals to ensure its continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness. Clause 9.3.2 lists the required inputs and 9.3.3 the required outputs. Documented information shall be available as evidence of the results of management reviews.

rows.name: Completing the audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.6 covers completing the audit, which occurs when the planned activities have been carried out and the report distributed. Clause 6.7 then addresses audit follow-up, which may extend past completion. Documents are retained or disposed of by agreement, and lessons for the audit programme are fed back under clause 5.7.

rows.name: Initiating the audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.2 covers initiating the audit: establishing contact with the auditee (6.2.2) and determining the feasibility of the audit (6.2.3). Establishing contact confirms authority for the audit, provides information on objectives, scope, methods and team composition, and arranges access. It is where the audit's terms are agreed rather than assumed.

rows.name: Control A.4.6 human resources
rows.description: Table A.1 control A.4.6 states that, as part of resource identification, the organization shall document information about the human resources and their competences used across the AI system life cycle, covering development, deployment, operation, change management, maintenance and transfer. Where selected, it produces a record that can be read against the competence determined under clause 7.2.

rows.name: Results of the management review
rows.description: Clause 9.3.3 requires the results of the management review to include decisions related to continual improvement opportunities and any need for changes to the AI management system, and requires documented information to be available as evidence of those results. A review that records attendance and discussion but no decisions has not produced what 9.3.3 asks for.

rows.name: Audit working documents
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.3.4 covers preparing documented information for the audit, and Annex A.13 gives guidance on working documents such as checklists, sampling plans and forms for recording evidence and findings. Annex A.13 also cautions that working documents should not restrict the audit activities, which can change as a result of information collected during the audit.

rows.name: A should cannot carry a nonconformity
rows.description: A nonconformity is the non-fulfilment of a requirement, as ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 3.16 defines it. A should expresses guidance rather than a requirement, so text in the should form cannot be the criterion a nonconformity rests on. The auditor who finds the substance sound but the criterion in the should form records an observation or an opportunity for improvement instead.

rows.name: Audit programme resources
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.4.4 covers the resources an audit programme needs, and clause 5.3 names insufficient time, equipment, training and competent auditors among the risks to the programme. Resourcing is where the risk-based approach becomes visible: concentrating auditor days on higher-risk processes necessarily thins coverage elsewhere, and the programme should record that choice rather than leave it implicit.

rows.name: Evidence types specific to an AI management system
rows.description: An AIMS audit draws on sources a general management-system auditor may not have sampled: documentation of data resources, tooling and computing resources, records of human resources and their competences, AI system technical documentation, event logs, impact assessment outputs and records of system operation and monitoring. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A control families A.4, A.6 and A.7 are where these originate.

rows.name: Audit feasibility
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.2.3 addresses determining whether the audit can be conducted at all: whether sufficient and appropriate information is available for planning, whether the auditee will cooperate, and whether adequate time and resources exist. A feasibility problem raised at initiation is a scheduling matter; the same problem discovered during fieldwork has already consumed the audit's time and the auditee's.

rows.name: Audit methodology and audit criteria are different documents
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 supplies the method: how to manage an audit programme, conduct an audit and evaluate auditor competence. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 supplies the criteria: the requirements an AI management system is examined against. A finding is raised against criteria, never against the method. Confusing the two produces a finding that cannot stand, because a guidance document contains no requirement capable of being unfulfilled.

rows.name: Audit programme records
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.7 addresses managing audit related records. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.2.2 separately requires that documented information shall be available as evidence of the implementation of the audit programme and of the audit results. The standard's requirement is the one a nonconformity can be raised against; the ISO 19011 guidance describes what good record management looks like.

rows.name: Feeding impact results into the risk assessment
rows.description: Clause 6.1.4 states that the organization shall consider the results of the AI system impact assessment in the risk assessment. The requirement is directional and it is a shall. Evidence that satisfies it shows the impact findings appearing in the risk assessment record; an impact assessment filed separately and never referenced leaves this requirement unevidenced even where both documents exist and are individually sound.

rows.name: Adjusting the plan during the audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.4.7 records that where the audit team becomes aware of new or changed circumstances, or of risks or opportunities, these should be addressed accordingly. A plan is a design, not a commitment to ignore what the evidence shows. Changes are agreed with the audit client and auditee and recorded, so that the report describes the audit that was actually conducted.

rows.name: Audit planning
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.3.2 covers audit planning: the plan describes the activities and arrangements for the audit and provides the basis for agreement among the audit client, audit team and auditee. Its detail should reflect the scope, complexity and the risks and opportunities of the audit. For an AIMS audit the plan is where the specific AI systems, virtual locations and evidence sources are named.

rows.name: Correction and corrective action
rows.description: A correction addresses the instance; a corrective action addresses the cause so the instance does not recur or occur elsewhere. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 10.2 a) covers the first and 10.2 b) the second, and they are separate obligations. Completing the missing documentation for one AI system is a correction; establishing why it was missing and whether other systems are affected is the corrective action.

rows.name: Objectives for an individual audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.2 states that each individual audit should be based on defined audit objectives, scope and criteria, consistent with the overall programme objectives. It lists what the objectives can include: determining the extent of conformity to the criteria, evaluating the management system's capability to meet statutory, regulatory and other requirements, evaluating its effectiveness in meeting intended results, and finding opportunities for improvement.

rows.name: Knowledge specific to auditing an AI management system
rows.description: Auditing an AI management system calls for knowledge a general management-system auditor may not hold: what an AI system is and what its life cycle stages are, what data provenance and data quality documentation look like, how an impact assessment differs from a risk assessment, and what evidence a tooling or computing resource control produces. The gap is usually in reading the evidence rather than in audit technique.

rows.name: Evidence of competence
rows.description: A job title is not evidence of competence and a headcount is not evidence that competence was determined. Clause 7.2 asks first what competence the work requires and then whether the people doing it hold it, on the basis of education, training or experience, with documented information available as evidence. The common gap is an AIMS that states a competence standard which the personnel records do not evidence.

rows.name: Clause 6.1.2 AI risk assessment
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 6.1.2 requires the organization to define and establish an AI risk assessment process that is informed by and aligned with the AI policy and AI objectives, is designed so that repeated assessments produce consistent, valid and comparable results, identifies risks that aid or prevent achieving the AI objectives, analyses those risks, and evaluates them. The requirement is on the process and its properties.

rows.name: Clause 7.2 competence
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 7.2 requires the organization to determine the necessary competence of persons doing work under its control that affects its AI performance, to ensure those persons are competent on the basis of appropriate education, training or experience, and where applicable to take action to acquire the necessary competence and evaluate the effectiveness of those actions. Appropriate documented information shall be available as evidence of competence.

rows.name: Every nonconformity traces to a requirement
rows.description: Before a finding is recorded the auditor identifies the requirement it rests on and confirms the requirement exists in the form claimed. ISO 19011 contains none, so nothing can be found non-conforming to it. Annex A controls apply where declared. Clauses 4 to 10 of ISO/IEC 42001:2023 are stated in shall throughout and apply in full. A finding that cannot name its requirement is withdrawn, not softened.

rows.name: Recording a conformity
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.18.2 asks that a record of conformity consider a description of or reference to the audit criteria against which conformity is demonstrated, the audit evidence supporting conformity and effectiveness where applicable, and a declaration of conformity where applicable. Clause 6.4.8 adds that where the audit plan specifies it, findings of conformity and of good practice should be recorded with their supporting evidence.

rows.name: The statement of applicability
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 3.26 defines the statement of applicability as documentation of all necessary controls and justification for inclusion or exclusion of controls. Clause 6.1.3 f) is the requirement that produces it. It is the document that converts the reference controls of Annex A into this organization's obligations, which is why a Table A.1 control becomes auditable only once it appears there as included.

rows.name: Recording a nonconformity
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.18.3 asks that a record of nonconformity consider a description of or reference to the audit criteria, the audit evidence, a declaration of nonconformity including a description explaining why the criteria are not fulfilled, any related findings, and the grade where grading is used. The three load-bearing parts are the criterion, the evidence, and the explanation of why the one does not meet the other.

rows.name: Reviewing documented information
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.3.1 covers performing the review of documented information before fieldwork: understanding the management system, gathering information to prepare audit activities and working documents, and forming a view of the extent of documentation relative to the audit objectives, scope and criteria. If what is supplied is inadequate the audit team leader should inform those responsible, and decide whether to continue or to suspend until the matter is resolved.

rows.name: Auditor competence
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 7.2 covers determining auditor competence, distinguishing personal behaviour (7.2.2) from knowledge and skills (7.2.3). Clause 5.4.2 addresses the competence of the individual managing the audit programme, and 5.5.4 the selection of audit team members. Clause 7.3 adds that evaluation criteria should be both qualitative and quantitative. All of it is guidance; the organization determines what competence its own programme requires.

rows.name: Audit results as a management review input
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.3.2 requires the management review to include, among its inputs, information on AI management system performance including trends in nonconformities and corrective actions, in monitoring and measurement results, and in audit results. Internal audit output is therefore not an end in itself: it is a named input to the review, and a management review record that does not reflect audit results leaves that element of 9.3.2 unevidenced.

rows.name: Selecting the audit criteria
rows.description: The criteria for an AIMS internal audit come from ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.2.1, which asks whether the management system conforms to the organization's own requirements for it and to the requirements of the standard, and whether it is effectively implemented and maintained. Both limbs are criteria: an audit that tests only the standard and not the organization's own AIMS requirements has audited half of what clause 9.2.1 names.

rows.name: Reviewing the AI policy
rows.description: Table A.1 control A.2.4 states that the AI policy shall be reviewed at planned intervals or additionally as needed to ensure its continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness. Like every Table A.1 control it applies where the organization has selected it under clause 6.1.3 and declared it in the statement of applicability. Clause 5.2 requires the policy to exist; A.2.4 is where periodic review of it comes from.

rows.name: Risk-based focus against evidence sufficiency
rows.description: The risk-based approach (4.8) directs effort toward significant matters; the evidence-based approach (4.7) requires that conclusions rest on verifiable evidence drawn from an appropriate sample. Concentrating hours on a high-risk AI system can leave another area sampled too thinly to support any conclusion about it. Nothing in ISO 19011 ranks the two, so the auditor resolves it by judgement and by stating plainly what the audit did and did not cover.

rows.name: Clause 4.1 context of the organization
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 4.1 requires the organization to determine external and internal issues relevant to its purpose that affect its ability to achieve the intended results of its AI management system, to consider the intended purpose of the AI systems it develops, provides or uses, and to determine its roles with respect to those systems. It also requires the organization to determine whether climate change is a relevant issue. All four are stated as shall.

rows.name: Auditing in a small organization
rows.description: In a small organization the only person competent to evaluate an AI system is often the person who built or operates it. ISO 19011:2026 anticipates this in clause 4.6 by carving out the case where internal auditors cannot be independent of the activity audited. The response is to name the constraint in the audit plan and record the safeguards applied, not to omit the area from scope or to present the audit as more independent than it was.

rows.name: Confidentiality against completeness
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 4.5 asks auditors to exercise discretion in the use and protection of information acquired during auditing, including proper handling of sensitive or confidential information. This can pull against the completeness that clause 4.3 asks for, particularly where evidence includes personal data or commercially sensitive model details. Nothing in the text ranks the two, and the usual resolution is to state the finding fully while holding the underlying evidence in the audit record rather than the distributed report.

rows.name: Clause 7.5 documented information
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 7.5.1 requires the AI management system to include the documented information required by the standard and that determined by the organization as necessary for the system's effectiveness. Clause 7.5.2 covers creating and updating it, and 7.5.3 covers its control. A note in 7.5.1 records that the extent can differ between organizations according to size, complexity of processes and competence of persons, so volume is not itself a measure of conformity.

rows.name: Annex A.6 AI system life cycle
rows.description: Table A.1 family A.6 addresses the AI system life cycle, including management guidance for AI system development and controls across life cycle stages. Its controls reach objectives for responsible development, life cycle processes, verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, technical documentation and event logging. Some carry an internal qualifier: A.6.2.6 asks that the organization define and document the necessary elements for ongoing operation, and states that at a minimum this should include system and performance monitoring, repairs, updates and support.

rows.name: Clause 5.2 AI policy
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 5.2 requires top management to establish an AI policy that is appropriate to the purpose of the organization, provides a framework for setting AI objectives, and includes commitments to meet applicable requirements and to continual improvement. The policy shall be available as documented information, refer as relevant to other organizational policies, be communicated within the organization, and be available to interested parties as appropriate. This is a clause requirement and applies whether or not control A.2.2 is selected.

rows.name: Audit programme objectives
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.2 states that the audit client should ensure audit programme objectives are established to direct the planning and conducting of audits, and that those objectives should be consistent with the audit client's strategic direction and context and support its management system policies and objectives. The clause lists what they can be based on, including the needs and expectations of interested parties, management system requirements, the auditee's level of performance, and the need to evaluate organizations in the supply chain.

rows.name: Technical expert on the audit team
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.15 defines the audit team as one or more persons conducting an audit, supported if needed by technical experts, and clause 3.17 defines a technical expert as a person who provides specific knowledge or expertise to the audit team. A technical expert supplies subject-matter understanding and does not act as an auditor. Bringing a data scientist onto the team to interpret model evaluation evidence is the intended use; having that person audit their own team's work is not.

rows.name: Clause 8.1 operational planning and control
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 8.1 requires the organization to plan, implement and control the processes needed to meet requirements and to implement the actions determined in Clause 6, by establishing criteria for the processes and implementing control in accordance with those criteria. It further requires the organization to implement the controls determined according to 6.1.3 that relate to the operation of the AIMS, and requires that the effectiveness of those controls be monitored and corrective actions considered where intended results are not achieved.

rows.name: Risks and opportunities to the audit programme
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.3 records that risks and opportunities related to the auditee's context can affect the achievement of the audit programme's objectives, and that the individual managing the programme should identify them and present them to the audit client when developing the programme and its resource requirements. The clause lists risk sources including planning, resources, selection of the audit team, communication, implementation, records and their control, and monitoring and review. These are risks to the audit, not the auditee's own risks.

rows.name: Audit sampling
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 Annex A.6.1 describes sampling as what takes place when it is not practical or cost-effective to examine all available information, and defines it as selecting less than one hundred per cent of the population to obtain and evaluate evidence about some characteristic of that population in order to form a conclusion about it. It states the associated risk plainly: the sample is not necessarily representative, so the auditor's conclusion can differ from the one the whole population would have produced.

rows.name: Clause 6.1.3 AI risk treatment
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 6.1.3 requires the organization to define an AI risk treatment process that selects appropriate treatment options; determines all controls necessary to implement them and compares those controls with Annex A to verify that no necessary control has been omitted; considers the Annex A controls relevant to the chosen options; identifies any additional controls needed beyond Annex A; considers the guidance in Annex B for implementation; and produces a statement of applicability containing the necessary controls with justification for inclusion and exclusion.

rows.name: Audit client and auditee
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.13 defines the audit client as the organization or person requesting the audit, and clause 3.14 defines the auditee as the organization or the parts of it being audited. A note to 3.13 records that in an internal audit the audit client can also be the auditee, or the individual managing the audit programme. The roles stay distinct even when one organization fills all of them, and identifying who requested the audit is how the auditor knows to whom the report is owed.

rows.name: Documented information and evidence
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 uses documented information for both what the organization maintains, such as a policy or a process definition, and what it retains as evidence, such as the result of an impact assessment under 6.1.4 or the audit results under 9.2.2. When testing a clause the auditor reads which of the two it asks for: a requirement to define a process is met by the process definition, and a requirement that documented information be available as evidence is met by the record of it having run.

rows.name: Clause 6.1.4 AI system impact assessment
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 6.1.4 requires the organization to define a process for assessing the potential consequences for individuals or groups of individuals, or both, and societies, that can result from the development, provision or use of AI systems. The assessment shall determine the potential consequences of the system's deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse; shall take into account the specific technical and societal context and applicable jurisdictions; and its result shall be documented. The organization shall consider the results in the risk assessment referred to in 6.1.2.

rows.name: Clause 10.2 nonconformity and corrective action
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 10.2 requires that when a nonconformity occurs the organization shall react to it, taking action to control and correct it and dealing with the consequences as applicable; evaluate the need for action to eliminate the causes so it does not recur or occur elsewhere, by reviewing the nonconformity, determining its causes and determining whether similar nonconformities exist or could occur; implement any action needed; review the effectiveness of any corrective action taken; and make changes to the AIMS if necessary. Corrective actions shall be appropriate to the effects of the nonconformities encountered.

rows.name: What the standard requires of each audit
rows.description: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 clause 9.2.2 states that the organization shall plan, establish, implement and maintain an audit programme including frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning requirements and reporting; that when establishing it the organization shall consider the importance of the processes concerned and the results of previous audits; and that the organization shall define the audit objectives, criteria and scope for each audit, select auditors and conduct audits so as to ensure objectivity and impartiality, and ensure results are reported to relevant managers. Documented information shall be available as evidence of the programme's implementation and of the audit results.

rows.name: Bounded Autonomy
rows.description: granting autonomy only within explicit, safe limits.

rows.name: Pattern to Control
rows.description: translating an identified pattern into a preventive control.

rows.name: CI Baseline Measurement
rows.description: measuring the starting point so improvement can be shown.

rows.name: Continual Improvement Model
rows.description: a structured, repeatable approach to improving services and practices.

rows.name: Do not Automate a Broken Process
rows.description: fix or retire a flawed process before automating it.

rows.name: Failure Prediction
rows.description: forecasting a likely failure from patterns in operational data.

rows.name: Model Drift
rows.description: degradation of a deployed model's performance as conditions shift.

rows.name: Monitoring and Event Management
rows.description: observing services and managing the events (state changes) they emit.

rows.name: Automation Bias
rows.description: the tendency to over-trust automated output and stop checking it.

rows.name: Autonomy Levels
rows.description: how much an agent may decide and act without human approval.

rows.name: Data Quality in Ops
rows.description: poor or shifted operational data as a driver of AIOps failure.

rows.name: Deskilling Risk
rows.description: losing human capability by automating away the work that builds it.

rows.name: Event Correlation
rows.description: grouping related events so many alerts collapse into one actionable issue.

rows.name: Over Automation Risk
rows.description: the risk created by automating decisions that should retain human judgment.

rows.name: Risk Based Oversight
rows.description: matching the strength of oversight to the consequence of the action.

rows.name: Event Alert Threshold
rows.description: the level at which an observed event becomes an alert requiring attention.

rows.name: Autonomy Decision Factors
rows.description: the inputs that set a safe autonomy level: reversibility, stakes, confidence, oversight cost.

rows.name: Data Quality for AIOps
rows.description: AIOps and prediction are only as good as the operational data feeding them.

rows.name: Efficient Inference
rows.description: operational choices (caching, batching, smaller models for simple cases) that cut compute per request.

rows.name: Prediction Value Threshold
rows.description: the point at which prediction's benefit outweighs its cost and false-alarm burden.

rows.name: Right Sizing Model
rows.description: using a model no larger than the task needs, cutting waste without hurting outcomes.

rows.name: Transparency to Users
rows.description: being clear with users about AI's role in a service and its limits.

rows.name: Over Trust Correction
rows.description: designing against blind over-reliance, e.g., prompting users to verify high-stakes AI outputs.

rows.name: Transparency Action
rows.description: disclosing AI use, confidence, and limits so users can judge when to rely on the service.

rows.name: Cost and Risk
rows.description: value has two sides: costs/risks a service removes for the consumer, and costs/risks it imposes.

rows.name: Experience Measurement
rows.description: measuring service quality from the user's perspective: did they achieve their goal, and how did it feel.

rows.name: Experience vs Performance
rows.description: a service can meet every technical target and still deliver a poor experience; the two are measured differently.

rows.name: Monitoring AI Services
rows.description: an AI service must be monitored for behavior and output-quality drift over time, not only for up/down availability.

rows.name: Trust Transparency
rows.description: being open about what the AI is, what it does well, and where it errs is what makes trust calibrated rather than blind.

rows.name: Model Changed Underneath
rows.description: an external provider can update or deprecate a model, changing your service's behavior without your action; the dependency must be monitored and contracted for.

rows.name: Effectiveness check
rows.description: verifying that corrective action worked

rows.name: Policy communication
rows.description: making policy available and understood

rows.name: Retain risk
rows.description: accepting a risk within criteria

rows.name: Iso 27005 risk
rows.description: guidance on information security risk management

rows.name: Logging and monitoring
rows.description: recording and reviewing security-relevant activity

rows.name: Policy controls
rows.description: controls establishing and reviewing security policy

rows.name: Review inputs
rows.description: the information the review must consider

rows.name: Risk treatment plan
rows.description: the plan for implementing selected treatment

rows.name: Stage 1 audit
rows.description: the readiness and documentation review stage

rows.name: Stage 2 audit
rows.description: the implementation and effectiveness audit stage

rows.name: Correction vs corrective action
rows.description: fixing the instance against removing the cause

rows.name: Disciplinary process
rows.description: the process following a security policy violation

rows.name: Effectiveness evaluation
rows.description: judging whether controls achieve their intended outcome

rows.name: Information security policy
rows.description: the documented statement of intent and direction

rows.name: Management system maturity
rows.description: the progression from documented to genuinely operating

rows.name: Modify risk
rows.description: applying controls to change likelihood or consequence

rows.name: Review cadence
rows.description: the planned interval at which review occurs

rows.name: Service delivery monitoring
rows.description: ongoing monitoring of supplier performance against requirements

rows.name: Share risk
rows.description: transferring or sharing risk with another party

rows.name: Surveillance audit
rows.description: periodic audits during the certification validity period

rows.name: Audit findings
rows.description: conformities, nonconformities and observations arising from an audit

rows.name: Classification in practice
rows.description: applying classification to real content in the moment

rows.name: Control selection is risk driven
rows.description: controls are selected because risk treatment requires them

rows.name: Control type
rows.description: whether a control is preventive, detective or corrective

rows.name: Incident response process
rows.description: the planned process for responding to security incidents

rows.name: Management review
rows.description: top management's periodic review of the ISMS

rows.name: Policy to practice
rows.description: how a written provision becomes a daily decision

rows.name: Review outputs
rows.description: the decisions and actions the review must produce

rows.name: Risk treatment options
rows.description: the four available responses to an evaluated risk

rows.name: Compensating control
rows.description: a control applied where the preferred one is unavailable

rows.name: Concentration risk
rows.description: exposure arising from many services depending on one provider

rows.name: Management system integration
rows.description: operating more than one management system on shared processes

rows.name: Risk acceptance criteria
rows.description: the thresholds at which a risk may be retained

rows.name: What to measure
rows.description: selecting indicators that reflect security performance rather than activity

rows.name: Auditor objectivity
rows.description: the requirement that auditors do not audit their own work

rows.name: Avoid risk
rows.description: not undertaking the activity that gives rise to the risk

rows.name: Likelihood and consequence
rows.description: the two dimensions from which a risk level is derived

rows.name: Classification survival
rows.description: whether a classification label persists when content is retyped or pasted

rows.name: Model level risk
rows.description: risks arising from a model treated as input-in, output-out

rows.name: Policy enforceability
rows.description: whether a stated rule can be observed, measured and acted on

rows.name: Risk assessment process
rows.description: the defined process for identifying, analysing and evaluating information security risk

rows.name: Risk register
rows.description: the record in which identified risks and their treatment are held

rows.name: Training data confidentiality
rows.description: the confidentiality exposure of data used to train or fine-tune

rows.name: Training data poisoning
rows.description: manipulation of training or fine-tuning data to alter model behaviour

rows.name: Agentic risk
rows.description: risks arising when a system plans, holds memory, calls tools and acts

rows.name: Autonomy and blast radius
rows.description: how the scope of possible damage widens with the degree of autonomy

rows.name: Monitoring and measurement
rows.description: determining what needs to be monitored and measured, and by what methods

rows.name: Risk owner approval
rows.description: the risk owner's acceptance of residual risk and the treatment plan

rows.name: Threat taxonomy ai
rows.description: published catalogues of AI-specific threats and their role as shared vocabulary

rows.name: Inference boundary
rows.description: the point at which organizational information crosses into a model provider's control

rows.name: Control attributes
rows.description: the attribute set that allows controls to be filtered and reported by different views

rows.name: Management system model
rows.description: the common structure of policy, objectives, processes and improvement shared across ISO management system standards

rows.name: Model as asset
rows.description: a model, its weights and its access path as an information asset in their own right

rows.name: Risk relationship
rows.description: how a threat exploiting a vulnerability against an asset produces risk, and how a control modifies it

rows.name: Risk appetite
rows.description: How much risk an organization is prepared to seek out or to hold on to, decided deliberately rather than discovered after the fact.

rows.name: Audit programme resources
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.4.4 covers determining programme resources, which include access to adequate and appropriate information and communication technology.

rows.name: Retention and confidentiality
rows.description: Audit records carry information the confidentiality principle protects, and their retention period and handling are determined rather than left to the auditor.

rows.name: Model weights and training data
rows.description: Both are information assets within the ISMS scope where the organization holds them, with confidentiality, integrity and availability properties of their own.

rows.name: Risk acceptance criteria
rows.description: Clause 6.1.2 a) 1) requires the organization to establish and maintain risk acceptance criteria, alongside criteria for performing risk assessments.

rows.name: Audit results as a review input
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.3.2 d) 3) places audit results among management review inputs, nested under feedback on information security performance.

rows.name: Accountability remains with the auditor
rows.description: Using a tool does not transfer responsibility for the conclusion. The auditor remains accountable for the sufficiency of the evidence supporting every finding.

rows.name: Testing an Annex A control
rows.description: Selecting evidence that would show whether the control operated as claimed across the period under audit, rather than at the moment of the audit.

rows.name: Audit follow-up
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.7 covers conducting the audit follow-up, including verifying completion and effectiveness of actions taken in response to findings.

rows.name: Policy availability and communication
rows.description: Clause 5.2 separately requires the policy to be available as documented information, communicated within the organization, and available to interested parties as appropriate.

rows.name: Review of documented information
rows.description: Named in clause 6.4.7. Establishes what the organization has decided and recorded, which is distinct from evidence that the recorded arrangement operates.

rows.name: Independence in a small organization
rows.description: Where few people hold the necessary competence, full independence from every audited activity may be unattainable, which clause 4.6 contemplates rather than prohibits.

rows.name: Feasibility of the audit
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 6.2.3 covers determining whether an audit is feasible, including whether the necessary access, cooperation, information and resources are available.

rows.name: Control effectiveness drift
rows.description: The gradual divergence between what a control was tested against and what the protected process now does, without any change event to trigger re-assessment.

rows.name: ISMS-specific auditor competence
rows.description: ISO/IEC 27007 offers guidance on the competence of ISMS auditors in addition to ISO 19011, covering the information security knowledge an ISMS audit requires.

rows.name: Model providers as suppliers
rows.description: An externally provided model or API enters the ISMS through the Annex A supplier-relationship controls, making the provider part of what the programme must cover.

rows.name: Audit-related records
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.5.7 covers managing audit-related records. Clause 6.4.7 requires audit evidence leading to audit findings to be recorded.

rows.name: Interested party requirements as input
rows.description: Requirements determined under clause 4.2 that the ISMS addresses can shape what the programme must give assurance about, particularly where they are contractual or regulatory.

rows.name: ISO/IEC 27001 as audit criteria
rows.description: In an internal ISMS audit, ISO/IEC 27001 functions as the criteria against which evidence is compared, alongside the organization's own requirements - not as the methodology.

rows.name: Control of documented information
rows.description: Clause 7.5.3 requires documented information to be available and suitable for use and adequately protected, addressing distribution, storage, control of changes, and retention and disposition.

rows.name: Re-performance
rows.description: Independently repeating a control step or calculation to establish whether it produces the result claimed. The strongest evidence of operating effectiveness and the most costly to obtain.

rows.name: Risk owners approval
rows.description: Clause 6.1.3 f) requires the organization to obtain risk owners approval of the risk treatment plan and their acceptance of the residual information security risks.

rows.name: Auditor competence elements
rows.description: ISO 19011:2026 clause 7.2 treats competence as personal behaviour (7.2.2) together with knowledge and skills (7.2.3), evaluated against criteria the organization establishes.

rows.name: Information security objectives
rows.description: Clause 6.2 requires objectives at relevant functions and levels, meeting seven stated requirements, and requires the organization to determine five things about how each will be achieved.

rows.name: The boundary of an ISMS audit
rows.description: A management system audit establishes whether arrangements are defined, operating and effective. Establishing whether a technical control resists a specific attack is a different activity requiring different competence.

rows.name: ISMS competence is not AIMS competence
rows.description: Competence records maintained for the ISMS do not evidence the competence an AI management system requires, because the necessary competence is determined against a different set of objectives.

rows.name: Objectivity in a first-party audit
rows.description: The requirement that findings and conclusions rest only on audit evidence, and not on the auditor's other interests in the audited area. Objectivity is established per assignment.

rows.name: The technical expert
rows.description: A person providing specific knowledge or expertise to the audit team who does not act as an auditor, and whose contribution does not by itself constitute audit evidence.

rows.name: Audit programme objectives
rows.description: What the programme as a whole is intended to achieve over its cycle, distinct from the objectives of any individual audit within it. ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.2.

rows.name: Design against operating effectiveness
rows.description: A control can be well designed and documented yet not operate, or operate for part of the period. Evidence that a control exists is not evidence that it ran.

rows.name: Annex A 5.35 independent review
rows.description: An ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control requiring the organization's approach to managing information security - people, processes and technologies - to be reviewed independently at planned intervals or on significant change.
